posts.caption:
Depreciation goes up by 10. Walk me through the three statements.

That's the real question. Anyone can name the three. What separates people is taking one line, changing it, and tracing it through all of them without stopping.

Net income falls 7.5, not 10, because the tax saving is real cash you keep.
Add the depreciation back and cash is up 2.5.
Assets fall 7.5, equity falls 7.5, and it balances.

Say "and it balances" out loud at the end. That's the sentence the interviewer is waiting for, and most people stop one line short of it.

State your tax rate before you start. 25% is fine. Picking one and saying it is part of the answer.

Save this for the night before.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #financialmodeling #accountinginterview

"Tell me about yourself" is the only question you know is coming. Most people still waste it.

90 seconds. 3 beats. One thread running through all of them.

Beat 1, where you started. 20 seconds, not 60. Where you're from, what you study, enough to place you. Then move.

Beat 2 is the only part they'll remember. One decision and what you did about it. A deal you followed, a club you joined, a model you built at 2am because you wanted to know how it worked. This is where a person shows up instead of a candidate.

Beat 3 points at the door. "Which is why I want to be in this seat, at this bank." It hands them the follow-up question you actually want.

Then cut it. A written answer of 220 words is about 90 seconds spoken. Most people deliver over 3 minutes and don't notice, because rehearsing in your head is always faster than saying it out loud.

Time it with a stopwatch. Once.

Save this.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #interviewprep #financecareers

Terminal value is 60 to 80% of your DCF. Most people spend 90% of their prep on the other 20%.

6 steps, in order. Project unlevered free cash flow for 5 years. Pick a WACC. Discount. Build terminal value. Discount that too. Bridge to equity.

Step 4 is where people fall apart.

Gordon growth takes your year 5 cash flow, grows it at g, and divides by WACC minus g. Keep g under long-run GDP growth, call it 2 to 3%. Quote 5% and you've just claimed the company eventually becomes the entire economy.

Two more things they're listening for.

Unlevered cash flow pairs with WACC. It's before interest, so it belongs to lenders and shareholders together. Pair it with cost of equity instead and you've counted the capital structure twice.

And a DCF gives you enterprise value, not a share price. Subtract net debt. Subtract preferred and minority interest. Divide by diluted shares. They asked for the share price.

Last thing. Don't call it the most accurate method. It's the most assumption-heavy one, and saying so is what makes you sound like you've built one rather than read about one.

Save this before your next technical.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #dcf #valuation

5 questions. Answer all five cold and you're ahead of most people in an investment banking first round.

The 3 statements. Enterprise value versus equity value. The DCF. Accretion and dilution. How a profitable company runs out of cash.

Every investment banking interview pulls from the same small set of technical questions. The names change, the order changes, the questions don't.

Each one here comes with the answer, and with the mistake that costs people the offer.

Two new technical questions every day, starting now.

Save this one for the night before.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #financecareers #valuation

A comp set isn't a list. It's an argument that the market should value your target exactly the way it values these 8 companies, so every name you include is a claim you have to be ready to defend out loud.

Screen on the business, not the label. Same model, similar size and growth, same geography, same customer. 2 companies can share an industry code and have nothing in common economically.

A sector screen isn't a comp set. It's 40 tickers.

Then pick the multiple the capital structure allows. EV/EBITDA ignores use, so it compares companies financed completely differently. P/E sits after interest, so debt contaminates it, and you should use it only where use genuinely matches.

Calendarise. A December filer and a June filer are 6 months apart.

Nobody mentions it until a VP does.

Use the median, never the mean. 1 outlier drags an average in a set of 8, so show the quartile range too and let the reader see how tight it actually is.

And explain your outliers rather than deleting them. The name trading at twice the median is the most interesting thing in the set.

Save this one.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #comparablecompanies

Your whole DCF rests on 1 number, and most candidates can't defend it.

WACC. Every term, and where each one comes from.

The weights are market value, not book. Equity weight uses market cap. Pulling book equity off the balance sheet is the single most common slip here.

Cost of debt is after tax. 100 of interest at a 25% rate costs the company 75, because the deduction is real. There's no equivalent on equity, since dividends aren't deductible. Haircut both and you've misunderstood why the haircut exists at all.

Cost of equity comes from CAPM. Risk-free rate, plus beta times the equity risk premium.

Beta isn't 1 number off a screen. Take your comps' betas. Strip out each company's use. Average the business risk. Re-lever at the structure you're modelling. That's 4 steps, and interviewers ask for all of them.

And use the current yield, not the coupon. A bond issued at 4% that now yields 6.5% costs you 6.5% to refinance. WACC looks forward.

Save this one.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #wacc #valuation

The market already priced it. So why does an acquirer pay 30% above that?

3 reasons, and only 1 of them is synergies.

Control. Buy 2% of a company and you have no say in anything. Buy 51% and you set strategy, appoint the board and direct the cash. A traded share price is what a minority stake costs, and control isn't in it. This is the reason most candidates forget.

Synergies, and say which kind. Cost synergies are overlapping functions and sites. You can count them and they usually land. Revenue synergies are cross-sell and new markets, they're forecast, and they frequently don't arrive. Buyers get discounted accordingly.

Scarcity. Sometimes there's no second asset like it, and that's worth paying for on its own.

Then the question underneath all 3. Who captures the value? If the acquirer pays away 100% of the synergies, the deal is great for the seller and does nothing at all for the buyer.

That's why most large acquisitions disappoint. Closing isn't the test.

Save this.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions #valuation

A company can post record profit and miss payroll in the same quarter. Here's how.

Revenue is booked when it's earned, not when it's collected. So a business growing 40% a year books profit on cash it hasn't seen yet.

Growth makes it worse, not better.

You buy inventory. You pay staff. You ship. You book the revenue. The customer pays you 60 days later, sometimes 90. Every extra unit of growth widens that gap, and you're the one funding it until it closes.

Then there are 3 more that have nothing to do with working capital. Capex outrunning operating cash. Debt coming due. A one-off legal or restructuring payment that lands in 1 quarter.

Here's the part almost everyone misses, and it's the part they're really asking about.

Where would you look?

The income statement is the last place this shows up. Operating cash flow falling while net income rises is the signal. Receivables up 50% on a 20% revenue increase is the cause.

So name the mechanism, name the line, name the statement. 3 sentences and you're done.

"Bad management" names nothing, and they move on.

Save this for the night before.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #financialmodeling

"Goodwill is the premium paid." That's the most commonly half-right answer in accounting, and half-right loses the question.

It's purchase price less the fair value of net identifiable assets acquired. Not book value. Fair value.

Here's why that distinction matters. Book value of net assets is 600. On acquisition, property and brands get written up and customer relationships get recognised for the first time, taking you to 750. You paid 1,000. Goodwill is 250, not 400.

The step-up happens first. The residual is what's left.

It's tested, never amortised. Finite-life intangibles get amortised. Goodwill sits on the balance sheet indefinitely and gets tested for impairment at least once a year. Amortising it over 10 years was the old rule and it hasn't applied for 2 decades.

And when it's written down, nothing leaves the building. The charge hits the income statement and equity. It's added straight back on the cash flow statement. Cash is untouched.

What it really is: the buyer admitting in public that it overpaid.

Save this one.

Most people say an LBO is buying a company with debt, then stop talking. That's the setup, not the answer.

5 steps. Sources and uses at entry. Project free cash flow. Sweep that cash against the debt. Exit on EBITDA times a multiple, usually after 5 years. Divide exit equity by entry equity.

So why use debt?

Take a 1,000 purchase funded 60% debt and 40% equity. Your cheque is 400, not 1,000. The same gain in enterprise value now lands on a much thinner slice, so a deal that would have returned 2.0x returns closer to 3.0x. Interest is deductible. And a repayment schedule keeps management honest.

Say the other half too. Use multiplies your losses on exactly the same maths, and if you don't volunteer that, they'll ask.

Returns come from 3 places and they aren't equally reliable. Debt paydown and EBITDA growth are things a sponsor can influence. Multiple expansion is a market call. Build on the first 2 and assume you exit at the same 10x you paid.

Good target? Steady cash flow, low existing debt, low capex. Not a software company growing 80% a year. It burns cash and it can't carry the debt.

Then finish with the number. Exit enterprise value, minus net debt, over your 400.

Save this one.

An increase in net working capital is a use of cash. Get that sign backwards and every forecast you build for the rest of your career is wrong in the same direction.

In: receivables, inventory, prepaid expenses, payables, accrued expenses.

Out: cash and short-term debt. Those are financing.

So the textbook version, current assets minus current liabilities, is the wrong number, because it quietly includes both of the things you were supposed to strip out.

Here's the mechanic. Receivables up 50, inventory up 30. That's 80 of cash sitting somewhere other than your bank account. Payables up 20 hands you 20 back, an interest-free loan from your suppliers. Net change: 60 used.

That's it. That's the whole thing.

The cycle in days is DSO plus DIO minus DPO. Days to collect, plus days of inventory, minus the days you take to pay, which is how long your cash is tied up before it comes home.

Some businesses run it negative. A supermarket collects at the till and pays suppliers in 45 days, so growth throws off cash instead of eating it.

Drop the term from your DCF because it looks small in year 1 and you've valued a company that never funds its own growth.

Save this.

posts.caption:
"Cash flow" means 4 different things. Each takes its own discount rate. Mix 2 of them up and your valuation is wrong by a mile.

Unlevered free cash flow. Start with EBIT of 200. Tax it at 25%, so 150. Add D&A of 40, subtract capex of 50, subtract a 10 build in working capital. That's 130, and it sits before interest, so it belongs to lenders and shareholders together. Discount at WACC. You get enterprise value.

Levered free cash flow. Start at net income instead, so after the 30 of interest. Same adjustments, then subtract mandatory repayment. That's what's left for shareholders. Discount at cost of equity. You get equity value, and there's no bridge to build.

Operating cash flow minus capex. The quick one, straight off the statement. It's levered, because operating cash flow already sits after interest paid. People feed this into a WACC-discounted DCF every single day and never notice.

Then EBITDA, which isn't cash flow at all.

It ignores capex. It ignores working capital. It ignores cash taxes and interest. That's 4 omissions, and if you call it a cash proxy you'd better be able to name all 4.

1 rule covers the whole thing. Match the claim to the rate.

Save this before your next model test.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #financialmodeling #valuation

posts.caption:
Why is there no P/EBITDA? 1 rule answers that, and every other multiple question you'll get.

The numerator and the denominator have to belong to the same people.

Enterprise value is the whole business, so it pairs with anything measured before lenders are paid. That's 4 of them: EV/Revenue, EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, and EV over unlevered free cash flow.

Equity value is the shareholders' slice, so it pairs with what's left after lenders. That's 3: P/E, price to book, and price over levered free cash flow.

P/EBITDA mixes them. Price is after debt. EBITDA is before it. The ratio describes nobody.

Here's why EV/EBITDA does the heavy lifting. Take 2 identical businesses. Company A has no debt and trades at a P/E of 20. Company B is heavily levered and trades at 12. Same operations, same 100 of EBITDA, and you'd conclude B is 40% cheaper. Their EV/EBITDA is identical, because enterprise value and EBITDA both sit above the capital structure.

Then say what EBITDA hides. Capex, working capital and cash taxes, all 3 ignored. For a capital-intensive business, EV/EBIT is often fairer.

Save this before your next technical.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #financialmodeling

"Which method gives the highest valuation?" There's a usual order, and the reason matters far more than the order does.

Precedents usually print highest. Comps sit below. The DCF ranges widest of the 4. An LBO sets the floor.

Why precedents beat comps.

A comp is what 1 share trades at, a minority stake with no say in anything. A precedent is what somebody actually paid to own all 100% of it and run it. That price carries a control premium, often 20 to 30%, plus whatever synergies the buyer talked themselves into.

Why the DCF ranges widest. WACC, terminal growth and your year 5 margin are 3 numbers nobody can verify, and a 1% move in any of them swings the answer more than a revenue assumption you'd argue about for a week.

Why the LBO is the floor. A sponsor needs its target return, so there's a hard ceiling on what it can pay. A strategic buyer with synergies goes higher.

Then say which one you'd lean on. Liquid comps, lean on comps. Live sale process, lean on precedents. Stable forecastable business, the DCF earns its place.

Say typically. Then say why.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #mergersandacquisitions

Somebody gave you 15 minutes. Most people waste 11 of them talking about themselves.

The first 60 seconds: thank them, name whoever connected you, 2 lines on you, and 1 on why you asked for this call specifically. Then stop talking.

Ask what only they can answer. "What's banking like" is a brochure question and you'll get a brochure answer. "How did you end up in this group" and "what surprised you in year 1" are questions nobody else can answer for them.

Show the reading without performing it. 1 specific reference, not 3. "I saw you worked on that deal, what was hard about it?" One is interest. Three is research, and it reads differently.

Minute 13 is the entire call. 2 questions: is there anyone else in the group worth speaking to, and is there anything I should be doing now. Both are easy to say yes to, and 1 of them hands you the next conversation.

Then follow up inside 24 hours, referencing something specific they said so it's obviously not a template.

Save this before your next one.

posts.caption:
Depreciation goes up by $10. You'll probably get the income statement right, and then lose it on cash.

Pre-tax income drops $10. At a 25% tax rate you pay $2.50 less tax, so net income falls $7.50, not $10.

On the cash flow statement you start from that -7.5 and add the 10 back, because depreciation is an accounting charge and not a single dollar of it actually left the bank. Cash ends up $2.50 higher.

That's the tax you saved.

Balance sheet: PP&E down 10, cash up 2.5, assets down 7.5. Retained earnings down 7.5. It balances.

If yours doesn't, check the tax line first.

Save this for your next technical round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #threestatements

Equity value to enterprise value. 4 adjustments, and you'll be asked why for each one.

EV is what the operations are worth to everyone who funds them, not just shareholders, so you add debt, preferred stock and minority interest, then take away cash.

Why subtract cash? Whoever buys the company gets it back.

Why add minority interest? If you own 80% of a subsidiary you still consolidate 100% of its EBITDA, so you add the 20% you don't own or your EV/EBITDA comes out too low.

Easy follow-up.

If the company issues $100 of new shares, EV doesn't move. Equity value and cash both rise by 100 and cancel.

Save it before your valuation questions.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #enterprisevalue

"Why investment banking?" Try this test on your answer: would it work just as well for consulting?

"A steep learning curve" fits consulting. "Smart people" fits law. "Passion for finance" fits nothing in particular. None of it's wrong. It just doesn't answer the question.

Build it in 3 beats instead. 1 moment that pulled you toward deals. 1 thing you actually did about it. Then why the analyst job itself is the next step, the modelling, the live transactions, seeing a deal from pitch to close.

Leave exit options out. They hear "I want to leave in 2 years."

Then say it out loud with a timer running. Under 60 seconds.

Which line in your current answer would fail the test?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #superday #financecareers

All-stock deal. Is it accretive? You can answer in 1 line if you compare the right 2 numbers.

Buyer trades at 20 times earnings and pays 15 times for the target, premium included, which means it's swapping expensive paper for cheaper earnings, so EPS goes up.

Flip them. Dilutive.

Cash deal? You compare the after-tax cost of that cash or debt with the target's earnings yield at the price paid. Yield is 1 over the P/E, so at 20 times it's 5%.

Then add the line I'd want to hear: accretive doesn't mean good. Overpay and EPS can still rise while value falls.

Save this one for M&A questions.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions #accretiondilution

A deferred tax liability is tax you've postponed. Not tax you've avoided.

Companies keep 2 sets of books and both are legal: GAAP for shareholders, tax rules for the tax authority, and depreciation is often faster on the tax side.

Say book depreciation is 10 and tax depreciation is 30. Taxable income is 20 lower, so at 25% you pay 5 less tax than your income statement shows.

That 5 is owed later. So it's a liability.

Later the accelerated depreciation runs out, cash tax climbs above book tax, and the DTL unwinds to 0.

On the cash flow statement, an increase in the DTL gets added back in operating cash flow. You recorded the expense but didn't pay it.

Save it for the accounting round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #deferredtax

Debt is cheaper than equity. So why doesn't every company borrow as much as it can?

Comment your answer first.

Debt is cheaper for 2 reasons: lenders get paid before shareholders, and interest is tax deductible. At a 25% tax rate, 100 of interest only costs you 75.

But every extra turn of debt puts more fixed claims ahead of equity, so shareholders' returns swing harder and they'll want more for holding the stock. Push further and default gets likelier, so lenders charge you more too.

And the shield? Worth 0 in a year with no profit.

Put it together and WACC falls, bottoms out, then climbs. A U. Your target structure sits near the bottom.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #wacc #corporatefinance

In a DCF, the terminal value is usually the biggest single number. Interviewers know it, so they'll push on it.

Perpetuity growth: final-year FCF times (1 + g), over WACC minus g. Keep g below long-run economic growth, or you've built a company that eventually becomes bigger than the economy.

Exit multiple: year 5 EBITDA times a multiple from today's comps.

Then use each to check the other.

Your growth rate implies a multiple, and your multiple implies a growth rate, so if 1 of them looks absurd you know which assumption to fix.

Last step, and people forget it: TV sits at the end of year 5, so you discount it 5 years.

Save this for DCF questions.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #dcf #valuation

"Where does your beta come from?" It's 4 steps, and you'll be asked for all of them.

Pull the levered betas for your comps.

Each one mixes business risk with that company's own debt, so you unlever them: levered beta over 1 + (1 - tax rate) x D/E. A beta of 1.2 with D/E of 0.5 and a 25% tax rate gives 1.2 / 1.375, about 0.87. Use market values for D/E, not book.

Take the median.

Relever it at the target's own structure. At a D/E of 0.3, 0.87 becomes about 1.07, and that's the number that goes into CAPM.

Save this with your WACC notes.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #wacc #beta

"Any questions for me?" Not the end of the interview. The last part of it.

Ask about their work. "Which deal taught you the most?" gets a real answer.

"What's a typical day like?" gets you the website.

Then ask what the group rewards, something like "what separates analysts who do well here?", because it tells you how they actually judge people and it shows them you're already thinking about being good at the job rather than just getting the offer.

Close the loop. "Is there anything in my background I can clarify?" is your 1 last shot at fixing a weak answer.

Prepare 4. Ask 2. Skip pay and hours.

What's the best question you've asked?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #interviewtips #superday

Why does every banker quote EBITDA? And what can't it see?

It's before interest, so you can compare 2 companies with very different debt loads, which is why it pairs with enterprise value and never with equity value.

It's before D&A too.

The blind spot is capex. Company A and Company B both have EBITDA of 100. A spends 10 on capex, B spends 60, so after that you're looking at 90 against 40.

It misses working capital and tax as well. A fast-growing business can post rising EBITDA while its cash disappears into receivables.

A comparison tool, not cash flow. Say both halves.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #ebitda #valuation

Prices are rising. LIFO or FIFO? Work it with 3 numbers.

You bought 1 unit at 10, then another at 14, and sold 1 for 20.

FIFO expenses the oldest cost: COGS 10, gross profit 10, tax at 25% is 2.5.
LIFO expenses the newest: COGS 14, gross profit 6, tax 1.5.

So LIFO shows less profit but keeps more cash, because it pays less tax.

FIFO wins on the balance sheet. Inventory sits at 14, closer to what it'd cost to replace. LIFO leaves it at 10.

Last point: IFRS doesn't allow LIFO. US GAAP does. Compare across the two and you adjust first.

Save it for the accounting round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #inventory

"Why our bank?" Run the swap test. Put a different bank's name in your answer. If it still works, rewrite it.

"A leading global franchise" passes for every bank on your list. That's the problem.

Name the group you'd join and what it actually covers.

Use 1 real conversation: who you spoke to, what they told you, why it stuck. It beats a paragraph of research.

Mention 1 deal the group worked on and why it interested you. 1, explained, not a list copied off their site.

Finish on fit. How the team works and why that matches what you've already done.

Does your answer pass?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #networking #superday

2 times your money in 5 years. What's the IRR? You should know it without a calculator.

MOIC is exit equity over entry equity. Put in 100, get 200, that's 2 times. It says nothing about time.

IRR does. 2 times in 3 years is about 26% a year. The same 2 times over 5 years is about 15%.

The 3 to memorise:
2 times, 5 years: about 15%
3 times, 5 years: about 25%
2 times, 3 years: about 26%

And don't divide. 100% over 5 years isn't 20% a year, because returns compound.

Funds report both numbers, because a quick flip can post a big IRR on a small gain.

#investmentbanking #privateequity #lbo #ibinterview

A company pays a $10 dividend. The trick is the statement where nothing happens.

Income statement: no change. You're distributing profit after it's earned, not paying an expense.

Cash flow statement: 10 out, in financing, next to buybacks and debt repaid.

Balance sheet: cash down 10, retained earnings down 10.

Then the follow-up they love, which is what happens to enterprise value, and the answer is nothing, because equity value falls by about 10 as the cash goes to shareholders and cash falls by the same 10.

The operations didn't change. Neither did EV.

Save it next to your depreciation walk-through.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #threestatements

$100 of revenue at a software company, or $100 at a grocer. Which would you pay more for?

Drop your pick in the comments first.

Revenue isn't profit. Grocers run on thin margins and software on high ones, so the same 100 of sales turns into very different cash for you as the buyer.

Growth moves the multiple. You're paying today for cash that arrives in year 3, 5, 10.

Durability too.

Subscription revenue that renews is far easier to forecast than sales you have to win again every year.

So I'd usually take software. But a slow, loss-making software company can be worth less than a steady grocer, so say "it depends", then say on what.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #multiples

How do leases change EBITDA? It depends on where the company reports, and that's the whole point of the question.

Since 2019 for listed companies, IFRS 16 and US GAAP's ASC 842 both put most leases on the balance sheet: a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.

Under IFRS 16, rent leaves operating costs and comes back as depreciation and interest. Both sit below EBITDA, so EBITDA goes up.

Under US GAAP, an operating lease keeps 1 straight-line cost inside operating expenses. EBITDA doesn't move.

So before you compare a European comp with a US one, check. If lease costs sit below EBITDA, lease liabilities belong in EV.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #ifrs16

Cost synergies or revenue synergies? Buyers trust 1 of them a lot more.

Cost synergies are what you can cut: a duplicate head office, 2 IT systems running side by side, 2 purchasing teams. Once the deal closes, they're in management's hands.

Revenue synergies are what you hope to sell.

Interest depends on debt, debt paydown depends on cash, and cash depends on net income, which depends on interest. Calculate interest on the average balance and you're right back where you started.

Unlevered or levered free cash flow? It comes down to 1 line: interest.

Unlevered is before interest. EBIT of 100 taxed at 25% is 75, plus D&A of 20, less capex of 30, less a $10 rise in working capital. That's 55, and it belongs to lenders and shareholders.

Levered is after interest. Take off 20 of interest after tax, which is 15, and you're at 40. That's what's left for shareholders.

Then match the rate. Unlevered at WACC gives you enterprise value. Levered at the cost of equity gives you equity value.

"What's your greatest weakness?" The perfectionist answer doesn't sound safe. It sounds like you'd hide a mistake.

Pick something real.

It shouldn't be core to the job, though. Speaking up in a room of 12 people works. Being sloppy with numbers, for an analyst role, doesn't.

Then 3 beats: the weakness in 1 sentence, 1 time it cost you, and what you changed.

Spend most of your 2 minutes on that last part, because they're listening for self-awareness and action.

And don't say it's gone. Say what habit you use now.

You calculate equity value per share and use basic shares. The interviewer's next question is about options.

The treasury stock method. Only count options in the money, with a strike below today's share price.

Say 10 options at a $10 strike, share price $20. Exercising them brings in $100. The method assumes the company uses that $100 to buy back shares at $20, so 5 come back.

Net new shares: 5. Basic 100 becomes 105 diluted.

A company is sold in bankruptcy for $500. It owes $400 of senior debt and $200 of subordinated debt. Who gets what?

Claims are paid in order. Senior first, then junior, then equity, and each class waits until the one above is paid in full.

Senior gets all 400. That's a 100% recovery.

The $100 left goes to subordinated lenders. 100 out of 200 is a 50% recovery.

Shareholders get 0.

That's also why junior debt pays a higher interest rate. It loses first when value falls.

Save it if you're interviewing for restructuring or credit.

Does growth always add value? Most people say yes. The answer depends on 2 rates.

ROIC is what the business earns on the capital it puts in. WACC is what that capital costs.

Invest 100 at a 12% return when capital costs 10%: you earn 12, pay 10, and keep 2 a year. As a perpetuity at 10%, that's about 20 of value.

Invest the same 100 at 8%: revenue and profit grow, and the company's worth less.

At exactly the cost of capital, growth adds nothing.

So in a DCF, if you raise growth, raise reinvestment too.

Save it for the valuation round.

#investmentbanking #valuation #dcf #ibinterview

A customer pays you $120 upfront for a year. Is that $120 of revenue? Not on day 1.

Your cash goes up $120 and so does deferred revenue, which is a liability. You owe them 12 months of service.

Each month you deliver, $10 moves from deferred revenue to revenue. The cash came in once.

On the cash flow statement, you add the increase in deferred revenue back in operations, since the cash arrived before the revenue did.

Is it debt? Usually not. It's settled by delivering the service, so it sits in working capital and stays out of your EV bridge.

Save it for the accounting questions.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #saas

Why is EV / net income the wrong multiple? 1 rule answers this one and every question like it.

EV is what you'd pay for the whole business, so it belongs to everyone who funded it. Lenders too.

That's why it pairs with numbers before interest: revenue, EBITDA, EBIT. Equity value is the shareholders' slice, and it pairs with numbers after interest, like net income, book value and levered FCF.

Mix them and you'll get nonsense. Take 2 companies with the same EV of 1,000 and EBITDA of 100. One has no debt, the other pays 30 of interest a year. At 25% tax (and ignoring D&A), net income is 75 against 52.5, so you get 13.3 times against about 19 times. Same business, different multiple.

Here's my quick test. If interest is already out of the denominator, you need equity value.

Save it before your next comps question.

You'll get a technical you can't answer. What they grade is the next 30 seconds.

Say what you do know: restate the question, name the concept it touches, and work from there. Most technicals tie back to the 3 statements, a DCF or an LBO, so start from whichever 1 it touches.

Think out loud. "My instinct is X, because Y" lets them steer you, and a corrected path still counts.

Then look it up that night and mention it in your thank-you email within 24 hours.

What's the technical that caught you out?

Paper LBO. No Excel, just a pen. What's the return?

Entry: EBITDA of 100 at 10 times is 1,000. Debt funds 600, the sponsor puts in 400.

Exit in year 5: EBITDA of 150 at the same 10 times is 1,500. Debt's been paid down to 300, so equity is 1,200.

1,200 over 400 is 3.0 times. Tripling in 5 years is an IRR of about 25%.

Where the 800 came from: 500 from EBITDA growth (50 at 10 times) and 300 from paying down debt. The multiple added 0.

Don't divide 800 by 5 and call it 40% a year. Returns compound.

What's the cost of debt in WACC? If you said the coupon, that's usually wrong.

The coupon was set when the bond was issued. WACC needs what lenders want today.

A 5% bond trading at 90 has a current yield of 5.6%, and its yield to maturity is higher still, because it's repaid at 100.

Then take tax off. Interest is deductible, so a 6% pre-tax cost at 25% tax is 4.5%.

No traded bonds? Use yields on debt with a similar credit rating, or add a spread to the risk-free rate.

And skip interest expense over book debt. That's history, not the market.

Save it for your WACC questions.

"Tell me about a deal you've followed." Most candidates recite the headline. Interviewers want your view.

Explain why the buyer wanted it, why the seller sold, and why now. Most people only cover the buyer.

Have the multiple paid and how it compares with peers.

Then say whether it's a good deal and name the biggest risk.

Which deal would you use?

Goodwill is impaired by $50. Before you answer, say your tax assumption out loud.

If it isn't deductible, net income falls by the full $50. You add the 50 back on the cash flow statement, so cash doesn't move at all, and goodwill and retained earnings both drop 50.

Balanced.

Now say it is deductible at 25%. It works like depreciation: tax falls $12.50, net income falls $37.50, and you end up with $12.50 more cash.

Under IFRS and US GAAP for public companies, goodwill isn't amortised. It's tested for impairment.

Save it for the accounting round.

How do you value a company with 2 very different businesses? You don't use 1 multiple.

You do a sum of the parts, valuing each division against its own peers.

Division A: EBITDA of 50 at 8 times is 400. Division B: EBITDA of 30 at 12 times is 360. That's an enterprise value of 760.

Debt and cash usually sit at group level, so you take net debt of 200 off once, at the end. Equity value: 560.

Head office costs don't belong to either division. Value them and subtract them.

If the market values the group below the sum, that's the conglomerate discount, and it's why spin-offs happen.

Save it for your valuation prep.

#investmentbanking #valuation #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions

Why can't you value a bank on EV / EBITDA? Because for a bank, debt isn't financing. It's inventory.

Deposits and borrowing are what it lends out, and interest is its cost of sales. You can't split operations from financing, so EV and EBITDA stop meaning anything.

Use equity multiples.

P/E, price to book, price to tangible book. If you want the intrinsic version, it's a dividend discount model.

P/B comes down to ROE against the cost of equity: P/B = (ROE - g) / (COE - g). Plug in an ROE of 12%, a cost of equity of 10% and 4% growth and you get about 1.33.

ROE equal to COE? P/B is 1.0.

Save it if FIG is on your list.

Subtract it.

Under the equity method, the company books its 30% share of profit as 1 line below operating profit. If the associate earns 100, that's 30 of equity income, and none of it's in EBITDA, which means your EV has to leave the stake out too or the multiple won't line up.

Equity value 1,000. Plus debt 300, less cash 100, less the stake worth 150. EV: 1,050.

It's the mirror of minority interest. Own 80% and consolidate 100%? Add NCI. Own 30% and consolidate 0%? Subtract the stake.

Save it with your EV bridge notes.

Why would a buyer pay for a target's past losses? Because they can cut future tax.

Net operating losses offset taxable income later. 100 of NOLs at a 25% rate is worth up to 25 of tax saved.

Up to. The company has to earn taxable income to use them, so value them year by year and discount what's saved.

In the US, federal losses from 2018 on don't expire, but each year they can offset at most 80% of taxable income.

After an acquisition, Section 382 caps how much can be used each year: the old company's value times a long-term tax-exempt rate.

Save it for your M&A prep.

Bankers read cold emails on their phones between calls. Write for that.

Subject line: a real connection plus the ask. Your shared university gets it opened. "Quick question" doesn't.

Body: 4 sentences. Who you are, why them specifically, 1 ask for a 15 minute call, and when you're free.

Keep the ask small. A short call is an easy yes. A referral comes later, after a real conversation.

No reply in a week? 1 short nudge in the same thread. Then move on.

What's the subject line you'd use?

"Walk me through a merger model." 5 steps, in order, and the follow-ups get easier.

1. Price: the target's share price plus a premium, times its diluted shares.
2. Funding: cash, new debt or new stock. Each has a cost: interest you give up, interest you pay, or more shares.
3. Combine: buyer net income plus target net income, plus synergies, less funding costs and new D&A from write-ups. All after tax.
4. New share count.
5. Pro forma EPS against the buyer's standalone EPS. Up is accretive, down is dilutive.

Then say what it means for value, not just EPS.

Save it for the M&A round.

#investmentbanking #mergersandacquisitions #ibinterview #mergermodel

Maintenance or incurrence covenant? It's about when the test runs.

Maintenance covenants get tested every period, often every 3 months. Say the limit is 4 times debt / EBITDA, with 350 of debt. EBITDA falls from 100 to 75, use goes from 3.5 to about 4.7 times, and you've breached it without doing a thing. You'll see these in bank loans.

Incurrence covenants only run when you want to act, like raising more debt or paying a dividend. They're common in high-yield bonds.

A breach usually ends in a waiver or an amendment, for a fee or a higher rate. Not bankruptcy.

Covenant-lite loans drop the maintenance tests and keep the incurrence ones.

Save it for LevFin interviews.

#investmentbanking #leveragedfinance #credit #ibinterview

Your interview thank-you note is the last thing they read from you. Most are generic.

Send it the same day, within 24 hours, by email.

1 note per interviewer. A group email reads like a template.

3 sentences: thanks for their time, 1 specific thing you discussed, and why it confirmed your interest. Leave the full pitch out.

Then check the name and the bank twice. A wrong bank name from your last template undoes a good interview.

Save it for after your next superday.

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #superday #interviewtips

Inventory gets written down by $10. It walks exactly like depreciation, right up until they ask about tax.

Assume it's deductible. Pre-tax income falls $10, tax falls $2.50 at a 25% rate, and net income falls $7.50. On the cash flow statement you add the 10 back. No cash left. Cash is up $2.50.

Balance sheet: inventory -10, cash +2.5, retained earnings -7.5. Done.

Here's the follow-up that catches people, though: what if the tax rules only let you take the deduction later, when the stock is actually sold?

Then you haven't saved any tax yet. Cash doesn't move at all, and that $2.50 sits in a deferred tax asset.

Save it next to your depreciation walk.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #threestatements

You sell equipment with a book value of $50 for $60. The trap here is counting the cash twice.

The $10 gain is profit. At 25% tax, net income rises $7.50.

On the cash flow statement you take the gain back out of operations, because it isn't operating cash. Operations ends at -2.5, which is just the tax you paid. The full $60 goes into investing. Cash is up $57.50.

Balance sheet: cash +57.5, PP&E -50 (book value, not the price), retained earnings +7.5. Balances.

Save it for your accounting round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #cashflow

"Tell me about a time you worked in a team." Say "we" the whole way through and they learn nothing about you.

Pick a team with real stakes. A deadline that could actually be missed, a client or a professor who'd notice.

Then it's "I" for your part. The goal, your role, what you did. Keep "we" for the outcome.

Put the friction in.

A missed handoff, a disagreement on the approach, someone falling 2 days behind, and how you dealt with it without turning anyone into the villain. Finish on what happened and 1 thing you'd repeat.

Deal teams are small. They're picturing you on theirs.

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #superday #behavioralinterview

You spend $100. Capitalise it or expense it? Same cash out the door, very different-looking numbers.

Take it pre-tax, year 1, with a 5-year life.

Expense it and EBITDA drops 100. So does operating cash flow.

Capitalise it and EBITDA doesn't move. You book 20 of depreciation, add it back, and operating cash flow ends at 0, while the $100 shows up in investing as capex.

That's why analysts always check the policy. It flatters EBITDA.

Free cash flow (CFO - capex) is -100 either way. If 2 companies treat it differently, you'd compare FCF, not EBITDA.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #EBITDA

A $100 convertible bond converts into 5 shares. Is it debt or equity?

Either one. Never both.

Conversion price: $100 / 5 = $20. Share at $25? It's in the money, so add the 5 shares to the diluted count and take the bond out of debt. Share at $15? Nobody converts, so it stays as $100 of debt in the EV bridge.

For diluted EPS it's the if-converted method. Add the shares, and add back the after-tax interest too, because a converted bond stops paying it.

Counting it as shares and as debt is the mistake they're listening for.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #convertiblebonds

"Where do you see yourself in 5 years?" Say "private equity" and they hear that you're leaving in 2.

They're checking 1 thing.

Will you stay long enough, and work hard enough, to be worth the time it takes to train you? So start with the analyst years: learning the modelling, getting on live deals, being trusted with a bit more each quarter.

Then talk skills, not titles. Judgement on deals beats "MD by 30."

Keep it to 3 sentences. It's a quick check, not a life plan.

What would you say if they asked you tomorrow?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #superday #interviewprep

How do you value a company that loses money? P/E is a price divided by a loss. It means nothing.

So you move up the income statement: EV/EBITDA if EBITDA's positive, EV/Revenue if it isn't.

If it's expected to turn a profit in 2 or 3 years, use forward numbers.

Stretch the DCF too.

A 5-year forecast that ends while the company's still losing money won't tell you much, so you keep forecasting until margins settle and only then do the terminal value.

And check the funding. If it's burning cash it may need to raise more, which dilutes today's owners.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #DCF

What makes a good LBO candidate? Every answer comes back to 1 thing: can it pay down the debt?

Stable, predictable cash flow. Lenders lend against cash they can count on, so a cyclical business with lumpy years is a risk.

Low capex. Picture 2 companies with $100 of EBITDA, one spending $10 on capex and one spending $60. The first has $90 to put towards the debt. The second has $40.

Then room to improve, because hoping the exit multiple goes up isn't a plan: costs to cut, assets to sell, margins to raise.

And a clear way out. A strategic buyer, another sponsor, an IPO. You don't have a return until you've sold it.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #LBO #privateequity

"Why should we hire you?" Everyone dreads it, but it's the easiest question to prepare.

"Hard-working and detail-oriented" is what every candidate says. Evidence is what they remember.

Pick 3 traits the analyst job actually needs: work ethic for the hours, accuracy for models that have to be right, curiosity to learn fast. Back each with 1 short example from your own experience.

More than 3 and none of them stick.

Close with 1 line on why this team, right now.

Which 3 would you pick?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #superday #financecareers

Asset deal or stock deal. Same company, same price, very different tax bill.

In a stock deal you're buying the whole entity, and every liability comes with it. Lawsuits too. The tax basis just carries over.

In an asset deal you pick what you take, and the tax basis steps up to the price you paid. Pay $500 for assets with a $200 tax basis and you've got $300 more to depreciate for tax, so you pay less cash tax for years.

So buyers usually want assets. At a 25% tax rate, that extra $300 of deductions is worth up to $75 in tax saved over the years it's written off.

Sellers usually want stock. In the US, a C-corp that sells its assets can get taxed twice: once on the gain, again when the cash goes out to shareholders.

Save it for your M&A round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions #tax

Should the buyer pay in cash or stock? There's no single right answer. There's a right way to reason, and it takes about 4 steps.

1. Cash makes sense when the buyer has it, or can borrow cheaply, and it's confident in the target. Its own shareholders keep all the upside.

2. Stock makes sense when the buyer's shares look rich, the deal's too big for cash, or there's doubt about the target. The seller becomes an owner and shares the risk. You pay for that in dilution.

3. Ask what the seller wants. Cash is certain. Stock is a slice of what comes next.

4. Weigh the cost first, then who should carry the risk.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions #dealstructure

What's an earn-out? Part of the price, paid later, only if the business hits its targets.

It exists because the 2 sides disagree. The seller believes the forecast. The buyer doubts it. The earn-out pays only if it comes true.

You tie it to 1 clear metric, like revenue or EBITDA over 2 or 3 years. Vague targets end in disputes.

Under ASC 805 and IFRS 3 it's contingent consideration, booked at fair value at closing and usually remeasured through profit and loss.

Here's the catch. The seller doesn't run the business anymore, but gets paid on its results, so an earn-out often just delays the argument.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions #dealstructure

Buy back 10% of your shares and EPS goes up 10%. Nope.

Say a company earns $100 on 100 shares, so EPS is $1, and at 20x earnings each share costs you $20.

It spends $200 of cash to buy back 10 shares. Now it's $100 over 90 shares, about $1.11, which is up 11% and not 10%, because you're dividing by a smaller number.

Then there's the catch you'll get asked about. That cash was earning 5%, which is $10 a year, and after a 25% tax you've lost $7.50 of earnings. So it's really $92.50 over 90 shares. About $1.03.

Up about 3%. That's it.

Then they sell for $100. Same price.

A $100 bond pays 5%. Rates rise to 10%. What's it worth now? Not $100.

Say it has one year left. It'll pay you $105 at the end, and that number is fixed no matter what rates do.

But a new bond now pays 10%, so $100 buys you $110. Nobody pays $100 for your $105 when they can get $110.

So your price falls until it earns 10% too: $105 / 1.1 = $95.45.

With ten years left the same jump hits harder. $5 a year for ten years plus the $100, discounted at 10%, is worth about $69. Longer bond, bigger fall.

That's the whole rule in one line: rates up, prices down. The payments never change, only what they're worth today.

Her bakery sells $150 of bread a year. Flour, wages and rent cost $100, so a normal year makes her $50.

If you count the whole oven in year 1, profit looks like -$50. But she'll use that oven for five years, so it goes on the balance sheet and you spread it out: $20 a year of depreciation. Year 1 profit is $30.

Cash is a different story. The $100 left her account on day one, so her cash is down $50 this year.

Add up all five years and both come to $150. Same money, different timing. That's why you'll always want the income statement and the cash flow statement side by side.

You own 80% of a company. So why is all of its EBITDA sitting in your numbers?

Because once you own more than half, you control it, and control means you report the whole thing. Your own business makes $40 of EBITDA, the subsidiary makes $10, so you show $50. Not $48.

Here's the catch. Your share price only pays for your 80%. The other 20%, worth $20 in this example, belongs to outside owners. That's minority interest (you'll also hear noncontrolling interest).

So the bridge goes: $300 of equity, plus $100 of debt, minus $20 of cash, plus $20 of minority interest. Enterprise value is $400, and $400 / $50 is 8x.

Forget the minority piece and you'd get 7.6x. The company would look cheaper than it really is, because your EBITDA covers owners your EV left out.

Say you own 100 shares at $50. That's $5,000. After the split you hold 200 shares, but each one is now half as much of the company, so the price drops to $25. 200 x $25 is still $5,000.

Nothing about the business changed. Same profit, same cash. Earnings per share go from $2.50 to $1.25, so the stock still trades at 20x.

Think of it like a pizza cut into 16 slices instead of 8. You've got more slices, but your piece is exactly the same size. Even the dividend follows: $1 a share becomes 50 cents, on twice the shares.

You buy it for $75 and sell it for $100. Is your margin 25% or 33%? Both numbers are real. Only one is margin.

The profit is $25 either way. What changes is what you divide it by.

Margin divides by the price: $25 / $100 = 25%. It's the share of every sale you get to keep.

Markup divides by the cost: $25 / $75 = 33%. Same deal, bigger number.

That's where people get caught. A 50% markup on $100 of cost gets you a $150 price, and $50 / $150 is only a 33% margin. If you want to keep half of every sale, you need a 100% markup.

In a model, gross margin, EBITDA margin and net margin are all over revenue. Markup is over cost, so it always looks bigger.

Say the same money could earn 10% a year somewhere else, at the same risk. After one year that's $110. In year two you earn 10% of $110, so $11, and you're at $121.

The deal pays $120. Your other option pays $121. You'd be $1 behind.

Bankers flip it around: what's the $120 worth today? Divide by 1.1 twice and you get about $99.17. Pay $100 for that and the net present value is negative.

Getting more back isn't enough. It has to beat what the money could earn elsewhere.

Mia prints $100 of posters for a client who'll pay in 60 days. She pays $70 for paper and ink today.

The sale counts when the work is done, so this month shows $100 of revenue and $70 of costs. Profit: $30.

But nothing has come in yet and $70 has gone out. Cash: down $70.

The missing $100 sits on her balance sheet as a receivable, money she's owed. When the client pays two months later, her cash ends up $30 higher, the same $30 as the profit, just later.

Profit counts what you've earned. Cash counts what's come in. Grow fast on credit and you can be profitable and still run dry.

Company A has no debt. After $10 of depreciation it earns $40, and its shares are worth all $400, so its P/E is $400 / $40 = 10x.

Company B owes $300 at 5%. That's $15 of interest a year. It earns $25, and its shares are worth only $100. P/E: 4x.

Now price the whole business, lenders and shareholders together, and you get $400 / $50 = 8x EBITDA for both of them.

P/E mixes the business with how it's funded. EV / EBITDA doesn't.

Beta 2 means a stock swings twice as much as the market. Twice the return, then? Nope.

Say safe government bonds pay 4% and the market's expected to return 9%, so you'd think a stock that moves twice as hard should get you 18%. That's the myth.

Beta only doubles the part above the safe rate. That part is 9% minus 4%, so 5%, and twice 5% is 10%. Put the 4% back on and you land at 14%, a full four points under the 18% you might have guessed.

Expected return = safe rate + beta x the market's extra. That's CAPM. It's how bankers usually get the cost of equity for a DCF.

2% a month sounds like 24% a year. It's actually 26.8%.

Say you owe $100 on a card at 2% a month and don't pay a cent back for 12 months. Month 1 adds $2, so you owe $102. Month 2 charges 2% on the whole $102, which is $2.04. That extra 4 cents is interest on last month's interest.

It keeps going. By month 12 the interest is almost $2.50, and you owe $126.82, not the $124 you'd get from 12 x 2%.

The quick way: 1.02 to the 12th power, minus 1. That's the effective annual rate, and it's why a monthly rate times 12 always undersells what you pay over a year.

You end up with a $49 share and $1 of cash. That's $50, the same as before. It's cash moving from one pocket to the other, and if that dollar gets taxed you're a little behind.

Price before = price after + the dividend. A dividend moves value to you, it doesn't make any.

$10 of inventory gets written off and profit falls $7.50. So why is cash up $2.50?

Leo's shop (made up for this one) has $10 of winter jackets nobody will buy, so he writes them down to $0.

Income statement: it's a $10 expense, so profit before tax falls $10. At a 25% tax rate the tax bill's $2.50 lower, and net income falls $7.50.

Cash flow: no cash left the shop, since he'd paid for the jackets long ago. Start from the -$7.50, add back the $10 that wasn't cash, and cash ends up $2.50 higher than it would have been.

Balance sheet: inventory down $10, cash up $2.50, so assets fall $7.50. Retained earnings fall $7.50 too. It balances.

The $2.50 is just the tax he doesn't pay: $10 x 25%.

$120 comes in, and January's revenue is just $10. Where did the rest go?

A gym (made up for this one) sells a year's pass for $120, paid on 1 January, which works out at $10 for each month of gym time it now has to deliver.

Cash: all $120, day one.

Revenue: only what's delivered. So $10.

The other $110 sits on the balance sheet as deferred revenue. It's a liability. The gym still owes you 11 months of workouts, and every month $10 of that moves out of the liability and into revenue until, by December, the liability is $0 and revenue has reached the full $120.

Cash counts when it's paid. Revenue counts when it's earned.

You own 10% of a company. Then it sells new shares and you own 8%. Did you just lose money?

Say it's worth $1,000: 100 shares at $10. You hold 10 of them, so 10%, worth $100.

It sells 25 new shares at $10 and takes in $250, so now there are 125 shares, your 10 are 8% of them, and the company itself is worth $1,250.

Divide by 125. Still $10 a share.

Your 10 shares? Still $100.

The catch is price. Sell those 25 at $6 and only $150 comes in, which leaves $1,150 over 125 shares, $9.20 each, and your stake falls to $92.

A smaller slice of a bigger pie can be worth exactly the same. What decides it is the price the new shares go for.

You pay 2%, then 3%. Is that up 1% or up 50%?

Both.

Borrow $1,000 at 2% a year and you pay $20 of interest, but at 3% you pay $30, so the same move in the rate shows up as two different numbers depending on what you compare.

3 - 2 = 1. One percentage point.

$10 extra on $20? Half again. 50%.

Bankers dodge the mix-up by saying points, or basis points. One point is 100 basis points, so 2% to 3% is "up 100 bps".

Subtract two percentages and you get points. Divide the change by where you started and you get percent.
